error_modes.label: Altitude control on the vectors until established on final

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch change made for the turn onto the downwind vector without a matching power correction, did not maintain the altitude assigned by the controller before final descent. The aircraft went more than 300 feet low with the deviation still increasing, and the IP took the aircraft to re-establish the assigned level. SP did not reference the altimeter or the VVI at any point during the vectoring turns.
texts.1: SP, due to a trim setting left unchanged after the configuration change on the base leg, did not hold the assigned altitude during the vectors to final. Deviation reached the 300 foot limit of the standard and was reduced only after the controller and then the IP verbally prompted a check of the altitude. The aircraft was returned to the assigned level shortly before intercepting final.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the heading bug during each controller-issued turn, did not keep the pitch and power combination that held the assigned altitude. Deviation opened to about 230 feet, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP detected the trend on the altimeter and recovered the assigned level without IP input. The remaining vectors were flown on altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained every altitude assigned by the controller during the vectors to final within 150 feet. Level-offs were anticipated with a lead point and the altitude was held through each turn without a power correction being needed late. Deviations that appeared were removed as soon as they showed on the altimeter.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitudes on the vectors to final essentially exactly, with excursions no greater than about 40 feet through the turns and configuration changes. Each level-off was anticipated and required no correction after roll-out. The altimeter needle stayed effectively motionless while the heading changes were flown.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the assigned altitudes within the published tolerance, but the deviation sat near the 150 foot edge of the standard for most of the vectoring phase rather than being held closer to the assigned level. Corrections were applied in single late steps at the end of each turn. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch and power change at the start of each turn so the altitude error stays well inside the standard.

texts_at.0: SP flew the vectors to final with the IP calling the power and pitch change for each controller-issued turn on the first vector and prompting only the altitude check on the second. Matching a pitch change to the power a vectoring turn requires has not yet become an automatic response. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to set pitch and power together at the start of each turn without a call from the IP as the vectors become familiar.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the assigned altitude during the vectors to final with the deviation settling at the 300 foot limit, due to a pitch and power combination that was not matched to the vector turn until midway through it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set pitch and power together at the start of each turn so the deviation does not reach the 300 foot limit.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the assigned altitude on the vectors with the deviation settling at about 230 feet, due to attention held on the heading bug through the turn before the altimeter was rechecked. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to include the altimeter in the scan through every turn rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP maintained every assigned altitude on the vectors to final within 150 feet, due to one level-off correction applied a few seconds after the deviation first showed rather than at the start of the turn. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch and power change at the start of the turn rather than partway through it.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the assigned altitude during the vectors to final with the deviation settling at the 300 foot limit before the level was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP to check the altitude against the assigned value. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the altitude trend on the altimeter after the deviation reached about 230 feet and recovered the assigned level without prompting or intervention, with the remaining vectors flown on altitude. Checking the altimeter through the turn, rather than after roll-out, would keep that trend smaller still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.3: SP maintained every altitude assigned by the controller during the vectors to final within 150 feet, anticipating each level-off with a lead point so no power correction was needed late. The only refinement available is to apply that same lead point to the very first turn as consistently as the later ones. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitudes on the vectors to final essentially exactly, with excursions no greater than about 40 feet through the turns and configuration changes. There is little left to refine; every level-off is already anticipated rather than corrected into. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude discipline on the vectors.

texts.0: SP, due to roll-outs flown without a computed lead point on the assigned heading, did not fly the headings issued by the controller during the ASR approach. Heading error exceeded 10 degrees on final with no correction started, the controller repeated the correction twice, and the IP intervened to place the aircraft back on the assigned heading. SP did not use the HSI to detect the drift off the issued heading between corrections.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections applied in bank angles too large for the small heading changes issued on final, did not settle on the assigned headings. Heading error reached the 10 degree limit of the standard on each correction and was contained only after repeated controller calls and a verbal prompt from the IP. The aircraft was oscillating either side of the assigned heading through most of final.
texts.2: SP, due to a delay in starting each turn after the controller issued the new heading, did not track the assigned heading continuously. Error reached about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, before SP recognized it on the HSI and rolled out on the assigned heading without IP input. The subsequent corrections were taken up promptly.
texts.3: SP flew every heading issued by the controller and held it within 5 degrees throughout the approach. Turns were started immediately on receipt of the correction and rolled out on the assigned value with a suitable lead. No repeat of a heading instruction was required.
texts.4: SP took up each controller-issued heading at once and held it to within about 2 degrees for the whole of final. Corrections were made in small, damped bank inputs that produced no overshoot on roll-out. The controller issued no repeat and no correcting call for azimuth.
texts.marginal: SP flew the assigned headings within the published tolerance, but the error tended toward the 5 degree edge of the standard between corrections and the aircraft wandered slowly off each new heading once established. The trend was arrested only when the controller issued the next instruction. SP is expected to hold the assigned heading actively against drift rather than relying on the next controller call.

texts_at.0: SP flew the headings issued by the controller with the IP flying the roll-out lead point on the first correction and calling the bank angle for SP to fly on the second. Judging the lead point for a small controller-issued heading change has not yet been learned. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to judge and fly the lead point independently as the picture on the HSI becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP flew the headings issued by the controller with the error settling at the 10 degree limit, due to a roll-out lead point that was not computed for the small heading changes issued on final. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compute a lead point for every heading change so the error does not reach the 10 degree limit.
texts_at.2: SP flew the headings issued by the controller with the error settling at about 8 degrees, due to a delay in starting the turn after the controller issued the new heading. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to start every turn on receipt of the heading rather than after a short pause.
texts_at.3: SP flew every heading issued by the controller and held it within 5 degrees throughout the approach, due to one turn that was started a beat after the instruction before the standard lead was applied. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start every turn on receipt of the heading with the same lead used on the others.

texts_above.1: SP flew the headings issued by the controller with the error settling at the 10 degree limit before the heading was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the assigned heading. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the heading error reaching about 8 degrees and rolled out on the assigned heading without IP input, with the subsequent corrections taken up promptly. Starting the turn on receipt of the heading, rather than after a short pause, would keep the error smaller before it develops. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound heading discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.3: SP flew every heading issued by the controller and held it within 5 degrees throughout the approach, with turns started immediately on receipt and rolled out on the assigned value with a suitable lead. The only refinement available is to apply the same lead to the very first turn as consistently as the later ones. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed heading discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.4: SP took up each controller-issued heading at once and held it to within about 2 degrees for the whole of final, with corrections made in small, damped bank inputs that produced no overshoot on roll-out. There is little left to refine; every heading is already captured on the first roll-out. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional heading discipline on the vectors.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control on the ASR final

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed during the approach, did not maintain the computed final approach airspeed after the descent was started. Airspeed decayed more than 10 knots below the computed value with no power correction applied, and the IP added power and took the aircraft. SP did not identify the decay from the airspeed indicator before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed on the controller's azimuth calls, did not correct the airspeed as the aircraft descended. Airspeed reached 20 knots above the computed value at the 10 knot limit on the slow side of the following correction, and was contained only after the IP prompted a power check. The approach was flown to MDA with the airspeed still oscillating.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check interval that lengthened each time the controller transmitted, did not hold a stable power setting on final. Airspeed drifted to about 15 knots above the computed value, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, before SP saw it on the airspeed indicator and reduced power to recover it without IP input. The remainder of final was flown on speed.
texts.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow throughout the ASR final. Power was set for the descent and adjusted in small increments as the configuration and the descent rate changed. The airspeed indicator was included in the cross-check between every controller transmission.
texts.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed to within about 3 knots for the whole of final, including through the descent and the configuration change. Power corrections were small and anticipatory, and no speed excursion of consequence developed. The airspeed remained stable while every controller call was answered.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed within the published tolerance, but it sat close to the 10 knot fast edge of the standard for much of final and was brought back only when the descent rate had to be re-established. Power corrections were reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to shorten the interval between airspeed checks so the speed is held nearer the computed value.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final approach airspeed with the IP setting the power for the descent on the first approach and prompting the cross-check interval on the second. Working airspeed into the cross-check at the rate an ASR final demands has not yet become automatic. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to hold the cross-check interval on airspeed without a reminder as the scan develops.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed with the deviation settling at 20 knots above the computed value, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed on the controller's azimuth calls. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep airspeed in the cross-check between every controller transmission so the deviation does not reach the 20 knot limit.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed with the deviation settling at about 15 knots above the computed value, due to a cross-check interval that lengthened each time the controller transmitted. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to shorten the interval between azimuth calls and the next airspeed check.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow throughout the ASR final, due to one power adjustment made a beat after the airspeed indication had already started to move. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the power change from the descent rate itself rather than from the airspeed indication.

texts_above.1: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with the deviation settling at about 19 knots above the computed value before the cross-check interval was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the airspeed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP saw the airspeed drift to about 15 knots above the computed value on the airspeed indicator and reduced power to recover it without IP input, with the remainder of final flown on speed. Shortening the interval between controller transmissions and the next airspeed check would keep that drift smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power management on the final.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow throughout the ASR final, with the airspeed indicator included in the cross-check between every controller transmission. The only refinement available is to anticipate the very first power change with the descent rate itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power management on the final.
texts_above.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed to within about 3 knots for the whole of final, including through the descent and the configuration change, with power corrections small and anticipatory. There is little left to refine; every power change is already anticipated rather than reacted to. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding power management on the final.

error_modes.label: Altitude control at MDA and the no-descent-below limit

texts.0: SP, due to a descent rate carried into the level-off without a lead point, did not stop the descent at the published MDA. The aircraft went below MDA on an approach where no descent below that altitude is permitted, and the IP arrested the descent and levelled the aircraft. SP did not recognize the penetration of MDA from the altimeter until the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a late reduction of the descent rate as MDA was approached, did not level off close to the published minimum. The aircraft stopped 200 feet above MDA at the limit of the standard and was brought down to the correct level-off only after the IP prompted a check of the altitude against the approach plate. The level segment to the missed approach point was flown high.
texts.2: SP, due to a level-off started without reference to the descent rate then being flown, did not capture MDA closely. Level-off occurred about 160 feet above MDA, between the plus 100 and plus 200 foot values of the standard, before SP recognized the excess altitude and descended to the correct minimum without IP input, with no descent below MDA at any point. The level segment was then held accurately.
texts.3: SP levelled off at the published MDA within 100 feet above it and at no point descended below the minimum. The level-off was anticipated from the descent rate and the altitude was then held to the missed approach point. The altimeter setting and the published minimum were confirmed before the descent was started.
texts.4: SP captured MDA within about 30 feet above the published minimum and held it precisely to the missed approach point, with no descent below MDA. The level-off required no correction after the initial power and pitch change. The minimum was flown as briefed and confirmed against the approach plate before the final descent.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off within the published tolerance above MDA and did not descend below it, but the capture was about 90 feet high, close to the edge of the standard, and the aircraft settled onto the minimum only part way along the level segment. The lead point for the level-off was short for the descent rate flown. SP is expected to set the lead point from the actual descent rate so MDA is captured closer to the published minimum.

texts_at.0: SP flew the level-off toward MDA with the IP flying the pitch and power change for the level-off on the first approach and calling the altitude check for SP to fly on the second. Timing the level-off from the descent rate rather than from habit has not yet been learned. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to time the level-off from the descent rate independently as the picture becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP leveled off close to the published MDA with the deviation settling at the 200 foot limit, due to a late reduction of the descent rate as MDA was approached. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to begin reducing the descent rate earlier so the level-off settles closer to MDA.
texts_at.2: SP leveled off close to MDA with the deviation settling at about 150 feet, due to a level-off started without reference to the descent rate then being flown. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the level-off lead point from the actual descent rate rather than from habit.
texts_at.3: SP leveled off at the published MDA within 100 feet above it and at no point descended below the minimum, due to the level-off lead being set a fraction short for the descent rate in use. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to compute the lead point from the actual descent rate on every approach rather than most of them.

texts_above.1: SP leveled off close to the published MDA with the deviation settling at about 190 feet above the minimum before the level-off was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP for the pitch and power required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the excess altitude at about 160 feet above MDA and descended to the correct minimum without IP input, with no descent below MDA at any point. Setting the level-off lead point from the actual descent rate, rather than from habit, would remove most of that excess. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady altitude capture at MDA.
texts_above.3: SP levelled off at the published MDA within 100 feet above it and at no point descended below the minimum, with the level-off anticipated from the descent rate and the altitude then held to the missed approach point. The only refinement available is to compute that lead point on every approach as consistently as the others. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate altitude capture at MDA.
texts_above.4: SP captured MDA within about 30 feet above the published minimum and held it precisely to the missed approach point, with no descent below MDA and no correction needed after the initial power and pitch change. There is little left to refine; the lead point is already computed rather than estimated. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary altitude capture at MDA.

error_modes.label: Compliance with and read-back of controller instructions

texts.0: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, did not comply with the instructions issued by the approach controller. A heading and a descent clearance were both actioned incorrectly, the controller queried the aircraft twice, and the IP took over the radios and the aircraft to re-establish the approach. SP did not request a repeat of the instruction that had not been understood.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not comply promptly with the instructions given on the ASR. Two instructions had to be repeated by the controller before they were flown, and compliance came only after the IP prompted the response, with the resulting heading error at the 10 degree limit of the standard. The approach was completed with the controller leading the aircraft rather than the aircraft following the vectors.
texts.2: SP, due to a read-back given before the instruction had been fully received, did not action one controller instruction at the moment it was issued. The delay produced a deviation of about 8 degrees in azimuth, between the 5 and 10 degree values of the standard, which SP corrected without IP input after re-confirming the assigned heading with the controller. The remaining instructions were read back correctly and flown immediately.
texts.3: SP read back every controller instruction in standard phraseology and complied with it without delay. Headings, descent clearances and the approach sequence were actioned as issued, and no instruction required repetition. Radio work did not displace control of the flown parameters.
texts.4: SP handled the approach frequency in standard phraseology throughout, read back each instruction accurately and flew it immediately, with no query from the controller at any stage. Transmissions were short and timed so they did not interrupt the instrument cross-check. The controller was able to run the ASR without a single repeat.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all controller instructions and remained within the published tolerances, but several read-backs used non-standard wording and compliance followed the instruction by a noticeable pause. No deviation reached the edge of a standard, though the pattern of late responses left little margin on final. SP is expected to use standard phraseology and to begin the correction as the read-back is made.

texts_at.0: SP complied with the instructions issued on the ASR with the IP reading back the first clearance for SP to confirm and prompting each subsequent instruction as it was issued. Recognizing a clearance and actioning it from standard phraseology alone has not yet become consistent at this stage of training. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to read back and action clearances independently as the approach sequence becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP complied with the instructions issued on the ASR with one heading correction actioned only after the controller's repeat and heading error reaching 10 degrees, at the limit of the tolerance, due to non-standard phraseology that left the read-back incomplete against the actual instruction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read back each instruction in standard phraseology so no correction needs a repeat.
texts_at.2: SP complied with the instructions issued on the ASR with one instruction actioned a few seconds after it was transmitted and heading error reaching about 8 degrees, due to a read-back given before the instruction had been fully received. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to let the controller finish transmitting before starting the read-back.
texts_at.3: SP read back every controller instruction in standard phraseology and complied with it without delay, with heading held within 5 degrees of the value issued, due to one read-back that was slightly slow while the bug was being set. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to separate the read-back from the heading-bug setting so both are completed without competing for the same moment.

texts_above.1: SP complied with the instructions issued on the ASR, with one heading correction settling at the 10 degree limit before it was actioned. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP confirming the assigned value. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP re-confirmed the assigned heading with the controller after a read-back given before the instruction had been fully received and corrected the resulting deviation without IP input. Letting the controller finish transmitting before starting the read-back would remove the need for that confirmation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable radio discipline on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP read back every controller instruction in standard phraseology and complied with it without delay, with headings, descent clearances and the approach sequence actioned as issued. The only refinement available is to separate the read-back from the heading-bug setting so neither competes for the same moment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good radio discipline on the approach.
texts_above.4: SP handled the approach frequency in standard phraseology throughout, reading back each instruction accurately and flying it immediately, with no query from the controller at any stage. There is little left to refine; transmissions are already timed so they never interrupt the instrument cross-check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior radio discipline on the approach.

error_modes.label: Observance of published routing and altitude restrictions

texts.0: SP, due to an approach flown without reference to the published minimum altitudes for the segment, did not observe the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP and the approach manual. The aircraft was flown more than 300 feet below the published segment minimum while still being vectored, and the IP intervened to climb back to a safe altitude. SP did not compare the assigned altitude with the published restriction at any point.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent started on the controller's advisory before the aircraft was inside the segment where it was published, did not respect the applicable altitude restriction. The aircraft reached the 300 foot limit of the standard below the published segment altitude and was returned to it only after the IP called the restriction. The remainder of the approach was flown with the plate held rather than briefed.
texts.2: SP, due to a briefing of the approach that covered the final segment but not the intermediate restrictions, did not apply one published altitude limit at the correct point. The aircraft was about 230 feet low against the segment minimum, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP identified the restriction on the plate and climbed back without IP input. No further restriction was missed.
texts.3: SP flew the ASR within the routing and altitude restrictions published in the MAIP and the approach manual. The applicable segment minima were known from the approach briefing and each descent was started only where it was authorized. No restriction had to be recalled by the controller or the IP.
texts.4: SP observed every published routing and altitude restriction precisely, with the aircraft never closer than a comfortable margin to a segment minimum before the point at which descent was authorized. The approach plate had been briefed in full and the applicable limits were quoted from memory when queried. The vectors were flown entirely within the published protected area.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the published routing and altitude restrictions, but the aircraft was flown close to a segment minimum with the descent started at the earliest point rather than with a working margin. No restriction was violated and no deviation approached the edge of a standard. SP is expected to build a margin against the published minima instead of flying the approach at the limit of what is authorized.

texts_at.0: SP flew the ASR with the IP identifying the published segment minima on the descent and calling the altitude restriction at each point. Comparing the assigned altitude against the published restriction without a cue is not yet consistent at this stage of training. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to identify the segment restrictions from the plate without a call from the IP as the approach becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP observed the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP with one segment reached at the 300 foot limit below the published minimum before it was corrected, due to a descent started on the controller's advisory before the aircraft was inside the segment where it was published. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm the segment boundary against the plate before acting on an advisory descent.
texts_at.2: SP observed the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP with one restriction reached at about 250 feet below the segment minimum before it was corrected, due to a briefing of the approach that covered the final segment but not every intermediate restriction. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to brief every intermediate segment restriction with the same detail as the final segment.
texts_at.3: SP flew the ASR within the routing and altitude restrictions published in the MAIP, with the applicable segment minima known from the approach briefing and altitude held within 150 feet of each assigned level, due to one descent that was started at the earliest authorized point rather than with a working margin. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan a small margin into each descent rather than starting at the earliest authorized point.

texts_above.1: SP observed the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP, with one segment settling at the 300 foot limit below the published minimum before the restriction was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the published altitude. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the restriction on the plate after the aircraft ran about 230 feet low against the segment minimum and climbed back without IP input, with no further restriction missed. Briefing every intermediate segment restriction with the same detail as the final segment would prevent that gap from opening. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured routing discipline on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP flew the ASR within the routing and altitude restrictions published in the MAIP, with the applicable segment minima known from the approach briefing and each descent started only where authorized. The only refinement available is to plan a small margin into each descent rather than starting at the earliest authorized point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise routing discipline on the approach.
texts_above.4: SP observed every published routing and altitude restriction precisely, with the aircraft never closer than a comfortable margin to a segment minimum and the applicable limits quoted from memory when queried. There is little left to refine; the vectors are already flown well inside the published protected area. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate routing discipline on the approach.

error_modes.label: Sequence, checklist and configuration timing on the approach

texts.0: SP, due to workload management that left the checklist unfinished before the descent, did not execute the approach sequence as described in the flight manual and AFMAN 11-202 Vol 3. The aircraft was still unconfigured when the descent to MDA was started, airspeed went more than 10 knots below the computed value, and the IP configured the aircraft and took control. SP did not run the before landing items at any point on the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit work inside the turn to final, did not complete the required actions in the order and at the points prescribed. The configuration change was made after the descent had begun and the resulting speed excursion reached the 20 knot fast limit of the standard, contained only after the IP prompted the checklist. The approach was completed with the sequence recovered but never fully caught up.
texts.2: SP, due to a checklist started later than the briefed point, did not complete the configuration before the final descent was due. Airspeed rose to about 15 knots above the computed value, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, while the items were completed, and SP restored the correct speed and sequence without IP input. The remaining approach items were run at the briefed points.
texts.3: SP executed the approach in the sequence prescribed by the flight manual and the published procedure. Checklists were completed at the briefed points, the aircraft was configured before the descent was started, and the flown parameters stayed inside the standards while the items were run. No item required prompting.
texts.4: SP ran the approach sequence exactly as briefed, with each checklist completed ahead of the point at which it was required and the configuration established well before the descent. Cockpit work was distributed so that no phase of the approach carried a peak of tasks, and the flown parameters were unaffected throughout. The whole approach was completed without a single reminder.
texts.marginal: SP completed the approach sequence and all required checklist items, but several were run at the latest usable point and the workload was concentrated in the turn to final. The parameters stayed inside the standards, though the margin narrowed each time an item was completed late. SP is expected to move the checklist and configuration actions forward so the workload is spread across the approach.

texts_at.0: SP executed the approach sequence with the IP running the checklist on the first approach and prompting each remaining item, configuration and timing, on the second. The order and timing of the sequence items for an ASR final have not yet been committed to memory. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to complete the sequence from memory, without a prompt, as the approach becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP completed the approach sequence with the configuration change made after the descent had begun and airspeed running 20 knots fast of the computed value, at the limit of the tolerance, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit work inside the turn to final. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin the configuration change before the turn to final rather than inside it.
texts_at.2: SP completed the approach sequence with the checklist started a few seconds later than briefed and airspeed running about 15 knots fast of the computed value, due to workload from the standby instrument scan delaying the start of the items. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the checklist at the briefed point regardless of the scan workload at that moment.
texts_at.3: SP executed the approach in the sequence prescribed by the flight manual with checklists completed at the briefed points and airspeed held within 10 knots fast of the computed value, due to one item that was completed at the latest usable point rather than with margin ahead of it. error_modes.label: Configuration completed later than 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to the aircraft being configured well inside the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, did not have airspeed and trim stabilized when the descent was due. Gear and flap changes were still taking effect as the descent began, airspeed went more than 10 knots below the approach speed with the aircraft out of trim, and the IP took the aircraft and re-established a stabilized final.
texts.1: SP, due to configuration started at the FAF rather than 2 to 3 NM before it, began the descent with the trim still being chased. Airspeed rose to about 20 knots above the approach speed, at the limit of the standard, while the trim was set, and the speed was recovered only under IP direction on power and trim.
texts.2: SP, due to gear and flaps being selected later than the 2 to 3 NM point, had no time to stabilize airspeed and trim before descending at the FAF. Airspeed moved to about 14 knots above 110 KIAS, between the plus 10 and plus 20 knot values of the standard, while the trim change was absorbed, and SP recovered the approach speed without IP input.
texts.3: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, so airspeed and trim were essentially settled when the descent began. Speed stayed inside the standard, no more than about 8 knots fast and 4 knots slow of 110 KIAS, through the configuration change and the start of the descent.
texts.4: SP had gear down, flaps TO and the Before-Landing Checklist complete well before the 2 to 3 NM point and the aircraft trimmed for 110 KIAS ahead of the FAF. The descent was started from a fully stabilized state and airspeed varied by no more than about 3 knots. No trim input was needed once the descent began.
texts.marginal: SP configured just inside the 2 to 3 NM point and reached the FAF with the trim only just settled, so airspeed sat near the 10 knot fast edge of the standard as the descent began. Nothing exceeded the tolerance, though the descent was started while the last trim change was still being made. SP is expected to configure 2 to 3 NM prior to the FAF so airspeed and trim are stable before the descent.

texts_at.0: SP configured the aircraft ahead of the FAF with the IP selecting gear and flaps at the 2 to 3 NM point on the first approach and calling for the trim change on the second. Completing configuration and trim early enough to start the descent already stabilized has not yet become an established habit under this workload. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to configure and trim the aircraft at the 2 to 3 NM point without a call from the IP as the workload becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, with airspeed settling at about 20 knots above the approach speed while the trim was set, due to gear and flaps being selected a little later than the 2 to 3 NM point. texts_at.2: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, with airspeed settling at about 14 knots above 110 KIAS while the trim change was absorbed, due to gear and flaps being selected a little later than the reference point. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the trim change before the FAF rather than into the descent.
texts_at.3: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, holding speed inside the standard, no more than about 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow of 110 KIAS, due to the trim needing one small correction as the descent began. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the trim a final time immediately before the descent rather than during it.

texts_above.1: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF with airspeed settling at about 19 knots above the approach speed while the trim was set. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP for the torque and trim required. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recovered the approach speed without IP input after airspeed moved to about 14 knots above 110 KIAS during the configuration change, with the trim change absorbed before the descent affected the profile. Selecting gear and flaps at the 2 to 3 NM point on every approach, not most of them, would prevent that margin opening. There is little left to refine; the aircraft is already stabilized well ahead of the reference point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent stabilization technique.

error_modes.label: Descent gradient not calculated for step-down fix restrictions inside the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to descent gradients never being calculated for the step-down fix restrictions inside the FAF, did not plan the descent against the published altitudes. The aircraft passed a step-down altitude more than 300 feet low with the rate unchanged, and the IP arrested the descent and regained the published profile. SP had not identified the step-down fixes during the approach briefing.
texts.1: SP, due to no gradient being computed from altitude to lose against distance available, arrived at the step-down fix about 300 feet above the planned profile, at the limit of the standard. The rate then flown to make the following restriction had to be corrected on IP call, and the remaining altitudes were met only with repeated prompts on rate and distance.
texts.2: SP, due to descent gradients estimated rather than calculated from altitude to lose and distance available, did not fly a rate that matched the step-down restrictions. The aircraft was about 230 feet high against the planned profile, between the 150 and 300 foot values of the standard, before SP increased the rate and made the restriction without IP input.
texts.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF and flew a rate that met each published altitude. Profile error stayed within about 120 feet, inside the standard, and no restriction was approached from below. The rate required was briefed before the descent.
texts.4: SP computed the altitude to lose against the distance available for every step-down fix and flew each segment so the published altitude was reached at the fix with negligible error. Deviation from the planned profile stayed within a few tens of feet and no restriction was missed. The gradients were quoted during the approach briefing.
texts.marginal: SP met all step-down fix restrictions, but the rate was set from the altimeter alone rather than from a computed gradient, so the aircraft reached each fix close to the 150 foot edge of the planned profile. Every restriction was satisfied and none was penetrated. SP is expected to calculate the descent gradient for each step-down fix so the profile is flown rather than recovered.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent inside the FAF with the IP calculating the descent gradient for the step-down fixes on the first approach and calling the rate required for SP to fly on the second. Computing a descent gradient from altitude to lose and distance available has not yet become a reliable habit. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to calculate and fly the descent gradient independently as the calculation becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF, with the profile settling about 300 feet high before the rate was increased, due to the gradient being flown at a rate that was not rechecked against the distance remaining. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recheck the flown rate against the calculated gradient at each fix rather than only at the first.
texts_at.2: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF, with the profile settling about 230 feet high before the rate was increased, due to descent gradients estimated rather than calculated from altitude to lose and distance available. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to calculate, not estimate, the gradient for every step-down fix rather than only the first.
texts_at.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF and flew a rate that met each published altitude, with profile error staying within about 150 feet, due to one segment's rate needing a small increase to stay on the calculated gradient. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the full calculated rate from the start of each segment rather than adjusting into it.

The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the rate required. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP increased the rate after the aircraft ran about 230 feet high against the planned profile and made the restriction without IP input, with no restriction penetrated. Calculating, rather than estimating, the gradient for every step-down fix would prevent that margin from opening. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound descent-planning technique.
texts_above.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the step-down fixes inside the FAF and flew a rate that met each published altitude, with profile error staying within about 120 feet and no restriction approached from below. The only refinement available is to set the full calculated rate from the start of each segment rather than adjusting into it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed descent-planning technique.

There is little left to refine; the gradients are already quoted in the briefing rather than computed in the air. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional descent-planning technique.

error_modes.label: Flap setting and airspeed not adjusted for crosswind or gusty conditions

texts.0: SP, due to the final being flown at the standard configuration and speed in reported gusty conditions with none of the airspeed increase the technique allows, did not keep a working margin on the approach. The gusts drove the airspeed more than 10 knots below the approach speed with the aircraft in the full configuration, and the IP added power, adjusted the configuration and took the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to no allowance being made for the gust factor in the target approach speed, flew the final with the speed swinging on each gust. Airspeed reached about 10 knots below the approach speed, at the limit of the standard, and was contained only after the IP directed an increase in the target speed for the conditions.
texts.2: SP, due to the flap setting and target speed being left unadjusted for the crosswind and gusts, did not hold a stable speed on final. Airspeed dropped to about 8 knots below 110 KIAS, between the 5 and 10 knot values of the standard, before SP increased the target speed for the conditions and stabilized the approach without IP input.
texts.3: SP allowed for the gusty conditions with an increased target speed and the appropriate flap setting, and the airspeed stayed inside the standard through the gusts, no more than about 4 knots slow and 8 knots fast of the target. Power corrections remained small and the approach stayed stable to MDA.
texts.4: SP set the configuration and the target speed for the reported crosswind and gusts before the final and flew the approach with speed variations of about 3 knots despite the conditions. The gusts produced no divergence in speed or attitude and the aircraft was stable throughout the descent to MDA.
texts.marginal: SP made an allowance for the conditions, but the increase in target speed was smaller than the reported gust factor called for, so airspeed touched the 5 knot slow edge of the standard on the stronger gusts. The approach stayed inside the tolerance and was stable overall. SP is expected to size the speed increase to the reported gusts so the margin does not depend on the timing of a gust.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final in gusty conditions with the IP calling the increased target speed for the conditions on the first approach and prompting the flap setting adjustment on the second. Sizing a speed increase to a reported gust factor has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to size and set the gust allowance independently as the calculation becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP allowed for the reported gusty conditions with an increased target speed, with airspeed settling at about 10 knots below the approach speed on one gust cycle before the increase was fully established, due to the allowance being added a beat after the first gust rather than before it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set the full gust allowance before the first gust is felt rather than after it.
texts_at.2: SP allowed for the reported gusty conditions with an increased target speed, with airspeed settling at about 8 knots below 110 KIAS before the increase was fully established, due to the flap setting and target speed being left unadjusted through the first part of the final. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the flap setting and target speed for the conditions before the final rather than during it.
texts_at.3: SP allowed for the gusty conditions with an increased target speed and the appropriate flap setting, holding airspeed inside the standard, no more than about 5 knots slow and 10 knots fast of the target, due to the increase being sized a fraction smaller than the reported gust factor called for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the increase from the reported peak gust rather than the mean wind.

texts_above.1: SP allowed for the reported gusty conditions with the deviation settling at about 9 knots below the approach speed before the increased target speed was fully established. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP for the target speed required. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP increased the target speed for the conditions after airspeed dropped to about 8 knots below 110 KIAS and stabilized the approach without IP input, with the adjustment self-initiated. Setting the flap setting and target speed for the conditions before the final, rather than during it, would remove the need for that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid gust-management technique.

The only refinement available is to size the increase from the reported peak gust rather than the mean wind. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed gust-management technique.
